claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim "Do the near-perfect editing results reported in prior work survive realistic evaluation?" run a preregistered replication-and-stress test of ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and FT-L on the same base models used in the editing literature where feasible, such as GPT-2 XL and GPT-J-6B, using public datasets CounterFact, zsRE, MQuAKE/COMPKE-style multi-hop QA, Natural Questions or TriviaQA for unrelated factual QA, WikiText-103 for perplexity, and a small general-ability suite such as HellaSwag, ARC, BoolQ, and MMLU subsets from HuggingFace. Evaluate each edit not only on the canonical prompt, but also on paraphrases, reverse relations where applicable, multi-hop questions requiring the edited fact, neighboring entities that should not change, unrelated facts, and general LM capability before and after 1, 10, 100, and 1,000 sequential edits. Compare reported editing success, generalization, locality/specificity, portability, perplexity shift, and downstream benchmark deltas against the original papers' metrics. If high edit success persists under paraphrase, multi-hop, locality, and general-benchmark evaluation with no meaningful degradation as edits accumulate, this weakens the claim that prior results fail realistic evaluation. If canonical success remains high but paraphrase, multi-hop, locality, or general ability collapses, especially under sequential edits, this supports the claim. This experiment could be made less necessary by strong existing independent replications that already use the same models, edit methods, datasets, and realistic evaluation axes with full prompt-level outputs and edit-order controls.

To address subclaims "Are localized weight edits disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space?" and "Do localized weight edits propagate globally?" perform a geometric audit of edited models from the first experiment. For each base model, collect hidden states on a public calibration corpus such as WikiText-103 or C4 validation from HuggingFace, compute per-layer representation covariance/PCA bases before editing, then apply single and sequential ROME/MEMIT/MEND edits. Measure how the induced activation change Δh on edited prompts, paraphrases, neighboring facts, and unrelated calibration text decomposes across principal components, especially normalized change magnitude per eigenvalue bin. Also measure propagation by tracing Δh and logit changes across layers, tokens, unrelated prompts, and tasks; include causal tests that project out low-variance versus high-variance components during forward passes to see which components account for edit success and collateral damage. If edits produce unusually large normalized movement in low-variance directions, and those components causally explain broad logit changes or benchmark degradation, this supports a geometric limitation. If update effects are confined to high-variance/task-relevant directions and do not spread outside edited contexts, the geometric subclaim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released activation-difference datasets and causal PCA/projection analyses from prior work covering the same edit methods and model families.

To address subclaims "Does damage compound as edits accumulate?" and "Is a parameter-free approach a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback?" compare sequential parameter editing against a weight-unchanged external-memory baseline under the same edit stream. Build an edit memory from CounterFact/zsRE/MQuAKE edits, retrieve relevant edited facts with a public retriever such as Contriever or BM25 over the edit memory, and prepend a compact evidence statement to the prompt without changing model weights; verify unchanged weights by file hash/checksum before and after. Run the same edit counts and evaluations as in the first experiment, reporting edit accuracy, paraphrase/multi-hop success, locality, unrelated factual QA, general benchmarks, perplexity, latency, context-length cost, and failure modes. If the parameter-free system matches or exceeds parameter editing on realistic edit success and locality while preserving unrelated capabilities across many edits, it supports the claim that it is a serious alternative. If it works only for trivial direct prompts, fails badly on paraphrases or multi-hop reasoning, or has unacceptable retrieval/context costs relative to edited models, the alternative-approach subclaim is weakened. This experiment could be reduced in scope if existing public benchmarks already compare retrieval- or memory-based nonparametric editing against ROME/MEMIT/MEND under identical sequential-edit and capability-preservation conditions.
reference_experiments: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.
